chunks: Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya, from al-Hasan ibn Ali ibn Abdullah, from Isa, from Aban ibn Uthman, from Isma'il ibn al-Fadl al-Hashimi, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

I asked him: 'Camels are sold at the gate of the Mosque; is it appropriate for one of us to buy them and take them out?' He said, 'There is no harm.' And the person in Ihram, if he shoots a bird standing on a tree whose trunk is in the Haram (sanctuary), the compensation is incumbent upon him, even if its branches are in the Hal (permissible area). He narrated that.

key_terms.بَابُ الْمَسْجِدِ: The gate of the Mosque (referring to the boundary of the Haram)
key_terms.جَزَاؤُهُ: Its compensation (penalty for the hunted animal)
key_terms.لَا بَأْسَ: There is no harm / It is permissible

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on compensation for shooting a bird from a tree rooted in the Haram while in Ihram?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (AS) clarifies the permissibility of acquiring livestock near the mosque to facilitate their removal from the sacred boundary, addressing practical concerns of pilgrims. Furthermore, he establishes a precise jurisprudential rule for *jaza'* (compensation) when a bird is shot while perched on a tree rooted within the Haram, even if its branches extend into the Hal, emphasizing the sanctity of the root location. This ruling reflects the Shia scholarly emphasis on the physical geography of the Haram in determining legal obligations during pilgrimage.
